Fish detection, tracking and identity: visual occlusion tutorial

Source: vignettes/articles/identity-occlusion-tutorial.Rmd
identity-occlusion-tutorial.Rmd

A visible track number is not a fish identity certificate

The interactive synthetic explorer includes optional occlusion and ID-switch demonstrations. These are deliberately simple, deterministic animations of five invented paths. They illustrate the distinction between a visible label and a permanent biological fish identity; they do not emulate a validated detector or a statistical distribution of fish behavior.

Four different questions

Question Typical output What it does not establish
Is an animal visible? A detector box, confidence, species hypothesis That the box is correct without ground truth
Where is it across adjacent frames? Camera-local track ID Permanent animal identity
Does the same fish reappear after occlusion? A proposed identity match, with uncertainty Identity truth without independent review
Is it the same fish in another camera? Calibrated correspondence hypothesis Reliable fish re-identification without evidence

Try the interactive illustration

  1. Open the synthetic explorer. Choose Lesson 2: Missing fish observations to jump directly to frame 105.
  2. Use Simulate a missing observation (enabled in Lesson 2) and move the timeline around frames 90–125. One synthetic track temporarily disappears from observation. Its underlying invented path still exists, but observed positions are missing.
  3. Select Lesson 3: Track-ID confusion (or enable Illustrate an ID switch) and advance past frame 125 and inspect the labels for the first two display tracks. They can exchange observed labels without the underlying invented fish exchanging bodies.
  4. Choose Lesson 4: Compare camera projections to inspect synchronized schematic XY and XZ panels. Orbit the isometric view and compare coordinate projections; these are not real synchronized cameras or physically calibrated XYZ.
  5. Choose Lesson 5: Align an experimental event and jump to frame 150. The yellow event marker is an invented timestamp, not a treatment effect. View the arbitrary-unit movement-rate chart and answer the interpretation question.
  6. Toggle Illustrative detector boxes, adjust box-only pixel jitter, enable movement arrows, select a fish for focus, and experiment with playback speed and single-frame stepping. Jitter changes only drawn rectangles, not true synthetic coordinates.
  7. Export the teaching CSV (including underlying invented IDs, displayed labels and missingness) or SVG. Both exports are marked synthetic. Switch back to Lesson 1 to inspect the unperturbed deterministic scene.

The rendered label changes are pedagogical only; no tracker actually ran. The figure explicitly marks simulated missingness. The example must never be included as measured biological performance.

Auditing real research predictions

Compare predictions with independently adjudicated camera/frame truth. Report evaluated frames with and without detections; identity switches on occlusions; explicit coverage, accuracy and association metrics where scientifically defined. Group performance by density, shadows, species, camera view and track fragmentation. Report holdout provenance.

See video intake, research datasets, the evaluation contract, and the capabilities matrix.

Interpretation of the computed panels

Observed fish count: the number of displayed teaching observations at the current frame; hides missing F1 during the invented occlusion. Movement rate: Euclidean displacement between consecutive invented 3D points divided by the illustrative 1/30-second interval; displayed in arbitrary units per simulated second. Nearest neighbor: instantaneous distance in the invented 3D coordinate system. Event-relative time: time difference from the illustrative log at 5.0 seconds. No panel reports genuine fish welfare, model detection precision, calibration accuracy, or causal effects.

The top and side camera panels project the same synthetic coordinates without any lens model, window refraction, occlusion segmentation, or image-processing model. They are concept teaching aids only.
